**Qualification:** no rule was installed or evaluated here.

`docs/linux-setup.md:54–87` leads with `MODE="0666"` for every Yubico hidraw interface and every Yubico USB
device, then makes `0660` group access an alternative at 89–102. This grants access to every local user;
the USB rule is broader than the hidraw access these transports require. PC/SC uses its daemon/reader
driver path, described separately at 5–38. Existing package rules may already provide appropriate access.
The supported next step is to inspect the selected YubiKey node and distribution-supplied rules, then
grant access only to the intended user/group or active desktop session. A service needs an explicitly
managed group rather than an assumed interactive login ACL. Explain that `plugdev` is an example group
which the administrator must provide, and keep read/write requirements near the actual typed opens.

Original systemd 262 `udev(7)` defines OWNER/GROUP/MODE and rule matching; pinned Yubico Device Permissions
separates PC/SC, keyboard and FIDO access. The linked upstream `69-yubikey.rules` currently assigns
`ID_SECURITY_TOKEN`, rather than the guide's world-writable modes. That rule alone is not proof that
every distribution grants an ACL: the administrator must verify the resulting access in its deployment.
Those publications are configuration/API guidance, not a normative SDK permission mandate.

`LinuxFidoHidConnectionTests.Open_ReturnsInvocationWhileNativeIsHeld:23–36` drains the invocation in
finally, then awaits/disposes the returned connection outside it. If AssertResponsive throws, release can
finish a successful open but control skips disposal of that result. The rooted native owner/worker can
remain live. `HeldWrite...:39–70` similarly drains output in finally but only requests disposal inside the
successful assertion body. A failure before that request leaves the connection owner unclosed. In
`CancelDuringPreparation:95–117`, a pre-cancellation assertion failure can make finally's expected-cancel
assertion replace the primary error after a successful open. The OTP held-native helper at 23–40 instead
captures and disposes the opened result within finally and is a useful local pattern.

`LinuxHidRoutingTests.DiscoveryTimeout...LateOpenAndCleanup:154–190` releases its gate in finally but does
not independently await late work/recovery on every failing branch. Some reactor tests create/publish a
held poll token and make setup assertions before a cleanup finally; `PublishedFailedAdmission:38–80` is a
concrete example. A harness watchdog bounding a child limits test-process damage, while actual resource
drain must still be observed for any cleanup claim. Later worker-failure setup and direct synchronous
disposal witness already have stronger finally/independent-join cleanup; preserve those positive oracles.

**Qualification:** source only; allocation/start faults unexecuted.

`StartGeneration:73–92` obtains a manager before constructing Generation. If construction throws before
assignment, the catch has no local cleanup for that manager. Generation allocates its GCHandle before
constructing Thread (`335–342`), so failure during Thread construction can also leave its new root.
After `RegistrationAttempted=true`, any registration or `Thread.Start` exception intentionally retains
the rooted generation. With an unstarted thread, Stop returns at 107 and restart is refused at 54;
there is no late worker to perform cleanup. That is safety-biased retained uncertainty, not successful
teardown or the ordinary callback-timeout/late-drain recovery tested elsewhere.

`StartGeneration` also uses an unguarded Error logger in its catch. A throwing logger can bypass its
remaining pre-registration Cleanup/Status assignments; `HotplugSignals` may still attempt disposal,
which cannot clean an unstarted generation. Keep diagnostics failure distinct from native failure.

source_passage_excerpts:
**Qualification:** pending on every Windows architecture/device lane.

`HidConnectionSlot.OpenRawConnectionAsync:82–85` creates the synchronous report
connection before Task.FromResult. `FidoHidConnection.SendAsync/ReceiveAsync` and
`OtpHidConnection.SendAsync/ReceiveAsync` call SetReport/GetReport inline and ignore
their token. `WindowsHidReportAccess:214–224` opens FILE_FLAG.NORMAL; ReadFile and
WriteFile at 155/183 use a null OVERLAPPED pointer. There is no baseline
CancelIoEx/GetOverlappedResult import, native-pending request object, native I/O
admission gate, shared disposal task, or checked-close outcome in that owner.

A synchronous native call borrows SafeFileHandle through its generated marshaller.
.NET 10 SafeHandleMarshaller.ManagedToUnmanagedIn takes DangerousAddRef and releases
it on Free. Calling `_handle.Dispose()` at WindowsHidReportAccess:316 during a held
ReadFile can close managed admission while deferring the actual native close to
the last reference release. Windows report facade Dispose/DisposeAsync simply
forwards this call. RegisteredFidoHidConnection and RegisteredOtpHidConnection use
DisposalGate's default lease-on-failure policy; after the inner Dispose returns,
the registration can be released while the other thread is still in native I/O.
On a custom adapter's throwing Dispose, B1-C005's unknown-release case also applies.
The built-in path's missing release observation and the custom path's arbitrary
teardown contract remain distinct. Protocol guard drain can protect a correctly
owned session exchange, but direct raw calls and connection disposal on another
thread still need their own contract.

The SafeHandle protects the active native handle from premature physical close;
its protection does not extend the registry token automatically. This is a
source-backed ordering concern, not a captured Windows race. A caller's task
submission, method invocation return, actual native terminal status, reference
drain and release proof must be recorded separately in future tests.

source_passage_excerpts:
**Qualification:** pending Windows native fault lane.

WindowsHidDeviceListener.Stop:139–145 and Dispose(false):297–305 ignore
CM_Unregister_Notification's CONFIGRET and free the GCHandle regardless. Microsoft
documents that unregister waits for pending callbacks, prohibits calling it from
the callback, and reports success versus CR_* failure. Success therefore supplies
the native drain relevant to releasing callback state; simply invoking it supplies
no successful-unregister observation. Restart after such an error discards the old
registration identity. Start:59–125 has no disposed check: Dispose sets `_disposed`
and suppresses finalization, but a subsequent successful Start can allocate a new
registration that a later Dispose's early-return path leaves live. This conflicts
with IDeviceChangeListener.Start's ObjectDisposedException contract.

The weak GCHandle allows the target to disappear before finalizer unregister.
The static callback drops a collected target, but GCHandle recovery/Target access
and its diagnostic log precede the try at line 168; the catch's log can also throw.
Containment of all managed exceptions crossing the unmanaged callback boundary
needs its own evidence. A failed Start's logging paths can likewise throw before
ClearRegistrationState. These are failure-path candidates, not a claim that normal
successful CM registration leaks or that all finalizers are unsafe.

Microsoft's pinned cfgmgr32.h declares LPGUID for both interface-list calls;
Cfgmgr32.Interop:284–299 passes Guid by value. Microsoft's x64 ABI passes a 16-byte
aggregate indirectly, which can make this declaration happen to interoperate on

enumeration crash is inferred from this declaration mismatch.

CM_Get_Device_ID_Size's PULONG and the two property APIs' PULONG sizes are declared
as out/ref IntPtr (Cfgmgr32.Interop:214–235,324–350). Windows ULONG stays 32 bits
across its architectures. The address itself is pointer-width; the pointed-to
integer is not. Current property calls start with IntPtr.Zero, so writing its low
32 bits can leave a zero high half on little-endian x64; record the mismatch
without inventing a demonstrated allocation failure. CmPropertyAccessHelper also
parses the type from the first probe while discarding the second returned type,
decodes the whole allocated string including its NUL, and uses only Debug.Assert
for several exact-size expectations. Property mutation between calls and CR_BUFFER_SMALL
need explicit later policy/tests. CmDevice.GetDevicePaths performs only one size/read
pair; the original API recommends retrying when hotplug grows the list.

Microsoft hidsdi.h returns BOOLEAN (one byte) for the HidD_* functions. All seven
declarations in HidD.Interop use UnmanagedType.Bool (Win32 BOOL, four bytes).
Kernel32's ReadFile/WriteFile correctly use BOOL and must keep that different
representation. HIDP_CAPS' native fields are unsigned USHORT; managed short has
the same width but changes value semantics above 32767, including report lengths.
No exercised return-register corruption or huge-report device is claimed.

SCard.Interop:90/111 encodes groups and decodes readers with ASCII; Connect marshals
UTF-8. SCARD_READER_STATE allocates names with StringToHGlobalAnsi, while
GetReaderName decodes UTF-8. ASCII replacement loses every non-ASCII byte sequence
before grouping or Connect. On Windows the ANSI allocation is code-page-dependent;
Unix's ANSI convention is UTF-8. Published 1.18.1 pcsc.c forwards char* reader names
straight to the platform SCard macro and performs no UTF-8/UTF-16 conversion.
The inspected CMake/header/Windows script defines no UNICODE conversion route;
installed producer flags and its selected Windows A/W export remain unbound.
This is the bounded follow-up gap, rather than proof of every installed shim's
code page. B1's #18 allocation/free source resolution remains intact.

Managed SCARD_IO_REQUEST contains two four-byte values and reports its own size.
Published Native_SCardTransmit accepts `const SCARD_IO_REQUEST*` directly and
forwards it to native SCardTransmit, whereas the shim explicitly converts other
uint32_t counts and reader-state fields. The retained pcsc-lite header documents
two `unsigned long` PCI fields: on Linux LP64 that structure is 16 bytes, unlike
the managed eight-byte carrier. This is a conditional source-level ABI discrepancy
for that producer/header target, not a Windows error or a demonstrated failure
with this host's installed binary. Windows uses its own DWORD layout; do not
generalize Linux width to Win32 or macOS.

Reader-state pack(1), two pointer-width fields, three uint32_t values and 36 ATR
bytes match the published wrapper's NATIVE_SCARD_READERSTATE, rather than the
platform SCARD_READERSTATE. GetAtr copies AtrLength bytes from fixed[36] without
a production upper-bound check; malformed native length needs a separate safe
negative vector before broadening robust-buffer claims. Published status-shim
copies platform ATR storage width, rather than arbitrarily trusting a C# buffer.

WindowsHidReportAccess.SetFeatureReport and SetOutputReport allocate report-ID-prefixed
sendBuf arrays and leave them for GC after success or failure. GetFeatureReport and
GetInputReport copy payload from another allocated native buffer and leave that
staging array for GC. The typed adapters clear their own first send copy in
finally, but that does not erase the nested Windows sendBuf. The returned array
properly escapes to the caller; deterministic cleanup of that independent result
is the caller's responsibility. The issue applies when those arrays contain PIN,
token, secret-derived or plaintext data; ordinary status/public metadata alone
does not justify a blanket secret classification.

ReadFile/WriteFile use `!success || count != expected`, then translate the captured
Win32 error. A short *successful* call supplies no failure code. With a zero/stale
last error, ThrowExceptionForHR may fail to throw or report an unrelated error.
GetInputReport can then expose zero-filled suffix; SetOutputReport can appear
successful. Keep this explicit short-count handling question separate from actual
Windows HID driver guarantees and B5's framing rules.

109 decimal (0x6D). Its comment is a PC/SC remote-session explanation, while the

The shared SCard error class assigns Windows SCARD_E_UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE=0x80100022
and SCARD_E_UNEXPECTED=0x8010001F. pcsc-lite's original API explicitly uses
0x8010001F for UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE and says UNEXPECTED is never returned there.

that pcsc-lite result UNEXPECTED. Its SCARD_PROTOCOL.Raw=0x00010000 also differs
from pcsc-lite's raw=0x0004. Current built-in Tx selects T0|T1; no raw-protocol
failure is inferred without a caller. The exception constructor accepts long but
sets a 32-bit HResult; symbolic lookup expects the stored positive uint values,
so sign-extended external inputs need a documented raw-carrier policy as well.

B3's 37 IOReturn mismatches and CFNumber LP64 issue remain Mac findings, not
Windows diagnoses. PlatformApiException currently formats an int as X8 and keeps
the supplied native source label only inside Message; a negative int can preserve
the raw 32-bit bit pattern without endorsing an incorrect symbolic enum. No

clears that clone on failure/disposal and exposes largeBlobKey as a slice; the borrowed original survives.

**D:** Preserve direct-factory borrowing and device-extension hidden-connection ownership.
`IYubiKeyExtensions.cs:37–62` resolves only SmartCard, copies creation settings, invokes
the public direct factory and calls `OwnConnection` after success. Core binds before
SELECT, registers the initial protocol before setup, and publishes readiness only
after OpenPGP application-data parsing and logging finish (`OpenPgpSession.cs:101–155`).
Failure disposes/detaches the session; the device helper owns failed hidden opens.
The backend borrows the effective protocol and needs no competing disposal owner.

`OpenPgpSession.cs:399–414` clears the current KDF and calls base teardown in finally.
Core `ApplicationSession.cs:444–520` makes the ordering concrete: synchronous Dispose
enters that override before protocol drain; asynchronous Dispose awaits protocol and
owned-connection cleanup, then calls the same derived override in finally. Both clear
the current cache, including asynchronous teardown failure. This settles the historical
async-dispatch question for the inspected source; it supplies no whole-workflow lease.

**M/P:** Extend `PGP-IMP-003` with the actual KDF copy graph: ToBytes disposes individual
TLVs but `EncodeList(...).ToArray()` abandons the first complete encoding; SetKdf's
returned encoding has no clearing scope. Parse's DecodeDictionary allocates field
copies, then init setters clone salts/hashes; those dictionary copies are abandoned.
The F9 response owner likewise escapes as Data and is not cleared after parse. Initial
PIN hashes are authentication material; public algorithm/AID/certificate metadata has
a different semantic classification. Reuse `CORE-C-C005/C006` and `CORE-B6-C002/C007`.

Core ApduTransmitter clones returned transport bytes into ApduResponse without clearing
the transport array. Chained responses leave preceding response owners, and failures
have narrower accumulator cleanup. SCP adds protected/plaintext owners. Clearing the
final OpenPGP response reaches neither those producers nor previous fragments. B6 owns
those shared mechanisms; this return adds actual PIN/F9/import/decipher caller links.

source_passage_excerpts:
**D:** Link `CORE-B5-C006`, B6 continuation/recovery and C's notification ownership at
the actual sites. Certificate SELECT DATA→GET/PUT, attributes→generate/import→refresh,
VERIFY→6982 status query, two-mode Unverify, KDF lookup→derivation→VERIFY and the whole
reset sequence each span more than one Core exchange. Core refuses overlapping
logical exchanges; it supplies no exclusion or disposal lease for these full methods.
Post-exchange parsing/cache changes and presence callbacks are outside the guard.
Await complete public tasks before another operation or disposal, and keep borrowed
keys, memory and prompt services alive through their actual last use.

Presence uses cached slot UIF, one direct read if absent, cancellation propagation and
PolicyMayRequire fallback on other errors (`OpenPgpSession.cs:322–371`). Sign, Decrypt,
Authenticate and Attest use Sig/Dec/Aut/Att scopes. Request runs before crypto APDU.
Resolution uses None; device status failure maps Failed, including historical 6600.
A pre-admission token can prevent an exchange; an admitted SmartCard exchange runs
with None through chaining/SCP and waits for native completion. An outer WaitAsync
ending gives no permission to clear inputs, release claims or retry a mutation.

**D:** `.Reset.cs:25–97` checks reset feature, reads counters, attempts PIN blocking,
ignores E6/44 status, calls the existing backend's ReadInitialState, refreshes app data,
clears UIF overrides and drops KDF. It leaves inherited readiness/authentication state
and the effective version unchanged. No complete erasure postcondition is checked.
Preserve `PGP-IMP-005`, ATT persistence and fixed-policy recovery qualifications.

At an SCP-created session, reset commands use the retained secure graph. Reselect uses
`PcscProtocolScp.SelectAsync:87–109`, which sends plain SELECT through that graph without
discarding/re-establishing keys; the following GET VERSION and application read again
use secure Send. OpenPGP retains no creation SCP parameters for a reset handshake.
This is the actual caller for `CORE-B6-C003` and B5 readiness qualifications. Normal
plain-reset history and an IsAuthenticated flag provide no SCP-reset acceptance.

source_passage_excerpts:
**D:** `Backend/OpenPgpBackend.cs:67–91` accepts OK with at least three bytes and decodes
the first three as BCD. Every non-OK response, every short OK and caught ApduException
falls back to 1.0.0. The comment/instruction attributing fallback only to 6985 is too
narrow. Transport/other exceptions still propagate. This fallback can conceal unrelated
status/malformed-version causes; changing that policy is an M/P facet, not a prose fix.

`OpenPgpSession.cs:130–154` logs detected version, passes override-or-detected version
to configuration and never consults physical metadata. Feature accepts major zero;
Pcsc Configure's major-zero branch ignores ForceShortApdus and selects transport
extended capability/Yk43 ceiling. Stable overrides affect framing, feature checks,
NEO import form, SELECT DATA and algorithm-info workaround. Overrides do not skip
SELECT/version probes. Reset rereads but deliberately discards the version. An OpenPGP
AID version is the card specification version, a separate value again.
